summary: Describes extensions by which two optional fields, Key and Sequence Number, can be carried in the GRE header. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A GRE tunnel wraps packets so they can cross a network they were not written for. This RFC adds two optional fields to the tunnel header: a number that says which conversation the packet belongs to, and a counter that lets the far end put packets back in the order they were sent.

questions: what is the gre key field
what is the gre sequence number
how does gre handle out of order packets
how to secure a gre tunnel
subtitle: Two optional GRE header fields: one labels the traffic flow inside a tunnel, the other keeps packets in order.

tldr.problem: GRE tunnels carry any protocol over any network, but the header had no room to say which flow a packet belongs to, and no way to put reordered packets back in order.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds two optional fields to the GRE header, a four-octet Key that identifies a traffic flow and a four-octet Sequence Number that the receiver uses to order packets, together with two flag bits that say whether each field is present.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Standards Track document that updates the GRE specification in RFC 2784.

today: RFC 2890 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 2784, the specification of GRE itself, by adding the two optional header fields and the rules for using the sequence number.

sections.title: What GRE Does and What This Adds
sections.content:
GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation) specifies a protocol for encapsulating an arbitrary protocol over another arbitrary network layer protocol. The original GRE header has a small set of fields: a Checksum Present flag, a Reserved0 field, a Version field and a Protocol Type field, followed by an optional Checksum and an optional Reserved1 field.

This RFC describes enhancements by which two fields, Key and Sequence Number, can optionally be carried in that header. The Key field is meant to identify an individual traffic flow within a tunnel, and the Sequence Number field is used to maintain the order of packets within the GRE tunnel.

The RFC also defines one term for the requirements. To silently discard a datagram is to discard it without further processing and without indicating an error to the sender; the implementation should be able to log the error, including the contents of the discarded datagram, and should record the event in a statistics counter.
sections.plainLanguage: GRE is a way of carrying one protocol inside another, so that a packet can cross a network that does not know how to handle it. This RFC adds two optional fields to the wrapper: one that names the conversation a packet belongs to, and one that numbers the packets so the far end can restore their order.

sections.title: The Extended GRE Header
sections.content:
The proposed header adds two flag bits and two optional fields to the original one. After the Checksum Present flag come the Key Present bit and the Sequence Number Present bit, then the Reserved0 field, the Version field and the Protocol Type field; the optional Checksum and Reserved1 fields follow, and then the optional Key field and the optional Sequence Number field.

The Key Present bit is bit 2. When it is set to 1, the Key field is present in the GRE header; otherwise it is not. The Sequence Number Present bit is bit 3. When it is set to 1, the Sequence Number field is present; otherwise it is not. The two bits are chosen to be compatible with the earlier GRE specification in RFC 1701.

Because the fields are optional, a receiver can tell from the bits alone whether to expect them, and a sender that does not need them leaves the bits clear and the fields out of the header entirely.
sections.plainLanguage: Two extra flag bits say whether the two new fields are there at all, so a receiver knows how to read the rest of the header without any out-of-band agreement.

sections.title: The Key Field
sections.content:
The Key field holds a four octet number inserted by the encapsulator. The method by which the Key is obtained is beyond the scope of the document, so the tunnel ends agree on it in whatever way suits them.

The Key is intended to identify an individual traffic flow within a tunnel. Packets may need to be routed on context information that is not present in the encapsulated data, and the Key supplies that context: it defines a logical traffic flow between the encapsulator and the decapsulator. Packets that belong to a flow are encapsulated with the same Key value, and the decapsulating tunnel endpoint identifies the packets of that flow by their Key value.
sections.plainLanguage: The Key is a number that both ends of the tunnel agree on for one conversation. When a packet arrives, the far end looks at the number to decide which conversation it belongs to, even when the packet's own contents do not say.

sections.title: The Sequence Number and What the Receiver Does
sections.content:
The Sequence Number field is a four byte field inserted by the encapsulator when the Sequence Number Present bit is set. The receiver must use it to establish the order in which packets were transmitted to it. The intended use is to provide unreliable but in-order delivery. When the Key Present bit is set, the sequence number is specific to the flow named by the Key field. Packets without the sequence bit set can be interleaved with packets that have it set.

The sequence number ranges from 0 to (2^32)-1. The first datagram is sent with a sequence number of 0, and the number is a free running counter represented modulo 2^32. The receiver keeps the sequence number of the last successfully decapsulated packet; when the tunnel is established, that value is set to (2^32)-1.

When the decapsulator receives an out-of-sequence packet it should silently discard it. A packet counts as out of sequence when its sequence number is less than or equal to the sequence number of the last successfully decapsulated packet, and a sequence number counts as less than or equal when its value lies in the range of the last received sequence number and the preceding 2**31-1 values, inclusive.

A packet is in sequence when its sequence number is exactly 1 greater than, modulo 2^32, the last successfully decapsulated packet, or when its sequence number field is not present at all. Such a packet is decapsulated successfully.

A packet that is neither in sequence nor out of sequence shows a sequence number gap. The receiver may do a small amount of buffering to recover the original order, placing the packet in a buffer sorted by sequence number. When an in-sequence packet is received and decapsulated, the receiver should look at the head of the buffer to see whether the next in-sequence packet has already arrived, and if it has, decapsulate it along with any further in-sequence packets in the buffer; the last successfully decapsulated sequence number is then set to the last packet decapsulated from the buffer.

No packet should ever wait more than OUTOFORDER_TIMER milliseconds in the buffer. When a packet has waited that long, the receiver must immediately walk the buffer in sorted order, decapsulating packets and ignoring any sequence number gaps, until no packet that has waited longer than OUTOFORDER_TIMER milliseconds is left, and then set the last successfully decapsulated sequence number to the last packet decapsulated. The receiver may also cap the number of packets in any per-flow buffer, where packets with the same Key value belong to a flow. If a packet arrives that would push more than MAX_PERFLOW_BUFFER packets into a buffer, the packet at the head of that buffer is decapsulated immediately whatever its sequence number, the last successfully decapsulated sequence number is set to its sequence number, and the newly arrived packet may then go into the buffer.

The RFC notes that the sequence number is used to detect lost packets and to restore the original order of packets that the network reordered, and that it should be used accordingly. It is a good idea to avoid it when the protocol carried in the tunnel has its own in-order delivery or tolerates reordering. If only some instances of the carried protocol need in-order delivery, only the corresponding packets need to be sent with the sequence bit set. Reordering out-of-sequence packets may be done for better performance and tolerance of reordering, and a small reordering buffer may help when the higher layer uses stateful compression or encryption, since the state of that compression or encryption is reset by packet loss.
sections.plainLanguage: The sending side numbers its packets, and the receiving side uses the numbers to sort them back into order. A packet that arrives too late is thrown away, a packet that fits the next expected number is passed on, and a packet that arrives early waits in a small buffer for a while in case the missing ones turn up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is brief here, and the reason is specific. When the Sequence Number field is used, it is possible to inject packets with an arbitrary sequence number and so launch a denial of service attack.

To protect against such attacks, the IP security protocols must be used to protect the GRE header and the tunneled payload. Either ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) or AH (Authentication Header) must be used to protect the GRE header. ESP protects the IP payload, which includes the GRE header; AH authenticates the entire packet apart from the mutable fields. The RFC ends with a note that catches people out: the Key field is not involved in any sort of security, despite its name.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the sequence number is easy to forge, a tunnel that uses it has to be protected by IP security, with either ESP or AH covering the GRE header. The Key field carries no protection of any kind, whatever its name suggests.

items.text: The Key field is not involved in any sort of security, despite its name.

viz.caption: What the receiver does with each packet

items.label: DECAPSULATE
items.desc: The number is exactly one greater than the last decapsulated packet, or the sequence bit is not set.

items.label: DISCARD
items.desc: The number is less than or equal to the last decapsulated packet; discard it silently.

items.label: BUFFER
items.desc: Neither of the above: hold the packet briefly in case the missing ones arrive.
